record_type_quote:
The current study presented the results of a randomized
controlled replication of PEERS, a manualized, parentassisted intervention to improve friendships for 58 adolescents with ASD, the second largest number of participants reported in the ASD treatment outcome literature for
individuals 6–21 years-old (Reichow et al. 2012).

targets.authors: Laugeson, E. A., Frankel, F., Mogil, C., & Dillon, A. R.
targets.title: Parent-assisted social skills training to improve friendships in adolescents with autism spectrum disorders.
targets.evidence_quote:
Most hypotheses were supported in this study and were
also a replication of similar results found in the original
PEERS study (Laugeson et al. 2009).
targets.outcome_quote:
In contrast to the original PEERS study, the current
study did not find that friendship quality significantly
improved in the experimental treatment group.
Upon closer
examination, in the original PEERS study, the significant
friendship quality finding was due to the waitlist control
group demonstrating worse friendship quality over time
(Laugeson et al. 2009).
targets.outcome_reasoning: Authors report supported original findings but explicitly contrast friendship quality and nonsignificant parent-rated social skills; the concluding support for PEERS efficacy is not an overall claim that all original findings replicated.

reasoning: Independent new-sample randomized controlled replication of the original 2009 PEERS trial. The 2012 follow-up is cited for later improvement, not itself re-tested at follow-up here.
